name: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
description: Preprocess a rooted tree so that many "what is the kth ancestor of node u" queries can each be answered quickly.
why_hard: Climbing ancestor-by-ancestor per query is too slow at the given constraints, forcing the binary lifting sparse-ancestor-table technique (O(n log n) preprocessing, O(log n) per query).

name: Fools and Roads
description: Given many simple paths marked on a tree, compute how many times each edge of the tree is used across all the marked paths.
why_hard: Each path must be split at its LCA into two upward paths, applied as point updates that are only resolved into per-edge counts via a subsequent subtree-sum (difference-array) DFS — a two-step technique built on top of LCA.

name: Distinct Colors
description: Each node of a tree has a color; for every node, count the number of distinct colors among the nodes in its subtree.
why_hard: A naive per-node subtree scan is O(n^2); an efficient solution needs either small-to-large merging of subtree sets or an Euler-tour-based offline reduction (e.g., Mo's algorithm on the tour), both nontrivial.

name: Vasya and a Tree
description: Process offline update queries that each add a value to every vertex within a bounded depth inside the subtree of a given vertex, then report the final value at every vertex.
why_hard: "Subtree AND bounded depth" must be encoded via Euler tour entry/exit times combined with a per-depth difference-array trick, a step beyond the standard single-dimension Euler tour + Fenwick tree pattern.

name: Minimal Diameter Forest
description: Given a forest consisting of exactly two trees, add a single edge connecting them so that the diameter of the resulting combined tree is minimized.
why_hard: Requires knowing that the optimal connection point in each tree is its center (not an arbitrary node) and deriving the resulting diameter from both trees' original diameters — well beyond a plain double-BFS diameter computation.

name: Path Queries II
description: Support point-update and maximum-value-on-path queries between two arbitrary nodes of a tree.
why_hard: Arbitrary node-to-node path queries (not just root-to-node or subtree queries) on a general tree require heavy-light decomposition to break each path into O(log n) contiguous segment-tree ranges.

name: Fixed-Length Paths II
description: Count the number of paths in a tree whose length lies within a given range [a, b].
why_hard: Requires full centroid decomposition to enumerate, for every centroid, all paths passing through it in aggregate O(n log n) time, plus careful inclusion-exclusion to avoid double-counting paths through the same centroid.

name: Xenia and Tree
description: Support two online operations on a tree: repaint a given vertex blue, and query the minimum distance from a given vertex to the nearest currently-blue vertex.
why_hard: It is the canonical online centroid-decomposition problem — nearest-marked-vertex queries must be answered by maintaining auxiliary minimum-distance data at every level of the centroid decomposition tree, updated online after every repaint.

name: Lomsat gelral
description: Rooted tree with a color per vertex; for every vertex output the sum of all colors that are "dominant" (most frequent) in its subtree.
why_hard: The canonical introductory problem for the technique — naive per-vertex counting is O(n^2), and small-to-large merging of child color-count maps gets it to O(n log n).

name: Dominant Indices
description: For each vertex of a rooted tree, find the depth (relative to that vertex) that contains the most vertices in its subtree, breaking ties by smallest depth.
why_hard: Requires merging depth-count arrays across children — the classic setting where "small-to-large" beats naive array merging, since arrays being merged can be swapped/pointer-merged instead of copied.

name: GCD Counting
description: Given a tree with a number on each vertex, find the length of the longest path whose vertices share a GCD greater than 1, for every prime factor.
why_hard: Combines small-to-large merging of per-prime depth information with tree DP; a good example of merging non-trivial per-vertex maps rather than simple counters. (Mirrored at CF 990G, rating 2400.)

name: Graph and Queries
description: Process edge-deletion and "find-and-zero-out-max-in-component" queries offline by reversing time (edge additions) and merging component data with a DSU where the smaller structure (e.g. an ordered set) is always merged into the larger.
why_hard: Shows small-to-large merging generalized beyond trees — merging balanced BSTs/sets across DSU components in reverse-time processing, a step up from the standard subtree-only setting.

name: Kingdom and its Cities
description: Given a tree and repeated small subsets of "capital" vertices, find the minimum number of vertices to block so that no capital can reach any other capital, using only vertices near the given subset.
why_hard: The textbook auxiliary-tree problem — building the virtual tree (via LCA-closure) of only the queried vertices each time is what makes the total work near-linear in the sum of query sizes instead of O(n) per query.

name: Tourism
description: On a graph built from a tree with extra "back" edges forming simple cycles, compute for every vertex the maximum total vertex weight reachable via a walk that never repeats a road consecutively.
why_hard: Requires condensing cycles and building auxiliary/virtual-tree-style structures over a reduced vertex set to make an otherwise quadratic DP tractable.

name: Partial Virtual Trees
description: Count, for every k, the number of ways to repeatedly shrink a vertex set to a proper "partial virtual tree" (an LCA-closed subset) exactly k times until only the root remains.
why_hard: The problem statement literally defines the auxiliary/virtual tree closure property (LCA-closed subsets) and turns counting over that structure into a combinatorics + tree-DP exercise, making it an unusually direct test of understanding the technique's core definition.

name: Tree Isomorphism I
description: Given several pairs of rooted trees, determine for each pair whether the two rooted trees are isomorphic.
why_hard: The direct introduction to canonical-form hashing (AHU algorithm) — recursively computing a sorted-children canonical label per subtree and comparing root labels.

name: Tree Isomorphism II
description: Same as Tree Isomorphism I, but the input trees are unrooted, so a canonical root (e.g. centroid) must be chosen before canonical-form hashing applies.
why_hard: Forces the extra insight that unrooted-tree isomorphism needs a canonical rooting (via centroid, since a tree has at most 2 centroids) before AHU-style hashing is even well-defined.

name: Symmetree
description: Determine whether a rooted tree can have its children reordered at every vertex so that it becomes a mirror-symmetric tree.
why_hard: A disguised isomorphism check — a subtree is "symmetric" iff it is isomorphic to its own mirror image, so it directly tests canonical-form hashing plus matching canonical forms in pairs among siblings.

name: Regular Forestation
description: Find a vertex whose removal splits a tree into two or more pairwise-isomorphic ("identical") subtrees, and report the maximum possible number of pieces.
why_hard: The problem statement explicitly defines tree isomorphism via a bijection preserving adjacency, then requires efficiently comparing many candidate subtrees for isomorphism using canonical hashing rather than brute-force bijection search.

name: The Fair Nut and the Best Path
description: Each vertex of a tree holds a fixed amount of gasoline and each edge costs gasoline equal to its length to cross; starting anywhere, walk a simple path (or stay put) and find the maximum gasoline left at the end, given the tank may never go negative along the way.
why_hard: The "never go negative" constraint looks like it forces a much messier DP, but the key insight is that any prefix of an optimal path already keeps non-negative gas, so the standard tree-DP (best single downward chain per vertex, combined from the two best children) applies directly once you see why the constraint never actually binds.

name: Choosing Capital for Treeland
description: Given a tree whose edges are fixed one-way roads, choose a capital city minimizing the number of roads that must be reversed so every city becomes reachable from it, and report that minimum along with every city achieving it.
why_hard: A single DFS only computes the reversal cost for one fixed root; getting the cost for every possible root efficiently requires the classic re-rooting trick — derive each child's answer from its parent's in O(1) based on whether the connecting edge already points the right way, instead of re-running DFS from scratch for every candidate capital.

name: New Year Santa Network
description: On a weighted tree, maintain the expected value of the sum of pairwise distances over a uniformly random triple of distinct cities, and after each update that shrinks a single edge's length, output the updated expectation.
why_hard: The sum of pairwise distances over a random triple reduces, via a double-counting identity, to a multiple of the ordinary sum of pairwise distances over all vertex pairs, which in turn decomposes edge-by-edge as (subtree size) x (n - subtree size) x (edge weight) — so every edge-weight update only requires updating one precomputed term instead of touching any actual path.

name: Military Problem
description: Given a rooted tree where each vertex's children are visited in increasing index order, answer queries of the form "what is the k-th vertex visited in the DFS traversal starting at vertex u," or -1 if fewer than k vertices are visited.
why_hard: Since a DFS subtree occupies a contiguous block in the Euler tour (entry-time order with children sorted by index), each query reduces to indexing k positions into the precomputed tour starting at u's entry time — the whole difficulty is recognizing that reformulation rather than simulating a DFS per query.

name: Kay and Snowflake
description: Given a rooted tree and multiple queries each naming a vertex v, report the centroid of the subtree rooted at v — the vertex whose removal leaves no remaining component larger than half the subtree's size.
why_hard: Answering each query with an independent centroid search would be too slow; the fix is to observe that a subtree's centroid always lies on the chain of heaviest children starting from its root, so precomputing each vertex's heavy child lets you walk straight down from v to the answer in time proportional to that chain, not the whole subtree.
